transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

I've been having a really hard time staying focused on my work and daily tasks lately. It feels like I just can't sustain my attention on anything for very long, and it's starting to cause some real problems.
Have you struggled with these focus and attention difficulties since you were a child, or is this a relatively new change for you?

It's definitely not a new change; I've actually struggled with this since I was a kid, well before I turned 12. While I've always dealt with it to some degree, this current constant struggle has been really bad for about two years and two months now.
Along with the focus issues, do you often struggle with physical restlessness, fidgeting, or feeling like you are constantly on the go, both now and when you were younger?

Yes, I definitely experience that. I often feel a lot of internal restlessness and feel like I'm constantly "on the go," almost as if I'm driven by a motor. Even when I was a kid under the age of 12, I was always running around and climbing on things when I shouldn't have been.
Over the past two years, have you also been feeling consistently down, sad, or hopeless, or have you lost interest in activities you normally enjoy?

No, I haven't really felt consistently down, sad, or hopeless. I still enjoy my usual activities and hobbies when I can actually get myself to focus on them. My mood has been okay, it's just the focus and restlessness that I struggle with.
Besides the restlessness and focus issues, do you find yourself struggling with excessive, uncontrollable worry or anxiety about various everyday things?
No, I wouldn't say I struggle with excessive or uncontrollable worry. I don't really get anxious about everyday things, it's more just frustration with my lack of focus.

Based on the patient's denial of excessive, uncontrollable worry or anxiety about everyday things, Generalized Anxiety Disorder has been ruled out. The patient's presentation of both significant inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms dating back to childhood (prior to age 12) and persisting into adulthood strongly supports a diagnosis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation). No further questioning is needed.
